children.text: Two gravitating masses M and m move in coplanar circular orbits of radii R and r about their common centre O, with \(MR=mr\). A third infinitesimal mass \(\mu\) is placed in the same plane and rotates so its position relative to M and m is stationary. It is not collinear with them and does not perturb their motion. G denotes the gravitational constant.

nodes.alt: Original coplanar circular orbits of M, m and infinitesimal mass mu about their common centre O.

children.text: Find the angular velocity of the line joining M and m.
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to M in terms of R and r.
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to m.
Find distance \(\rho\) from \(\mu\) to the common centre.

Now take M = m. Give the infinitesimal mass a small radial perturbation along its line from O. Under the source's assumed conservation of its angular momentum, find the radial oscillation frequency in terms of \(\omega_0\).

children.text: The source describes three spacecraft at the corners of an equilateral triangle of arm length \(L=5.0\) million kilometres. Their plane rolls once per year as they orbit the Sun, trailing Earth by \(20^\circ\). Find the relative speed of two spacecraft in their common plane, using 365 days per year.

statement.text:
A Three-body Problem and LISA
Two gravitating masses M and m move in coplanar circular orbits of radii R and r about their common centre O, with \(MR=mr\). A third infinitesimal mass \(\mu\) is placed in the same plane and rotates so its position relative to M and m is stationary. It is not collinear with them and does not perturb their motion. G denotes the gravitational constant.

1.1. Binary angular velocity
Find the angular velocity of the line joining M and m.
1.2.1. Distance to M
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to M in terms of R and r.
1.2.2. Distance to m
Find the distance from \(\mu\) to m.
1.2.3. Distance to O
Find distance \(\rho\) from \(\mu\) to the common centre.
1.3. Restricted radial oscillation
Now take M = m. Give the infinitesimal mass a small radial perturbation along its line from O. Under the source's assumed conservation of its angular momentum, find the radial oscillation frequency in terms of \(\omega_0\).
1.4. LISA relative speed

The source describes three spacecraft at the corners of an equilateral triangle of arm length \(L=5.0\) million kilometres. Their plane rolls once per year as they orbit the Sun, trailing Earth by \(20^\circ\). Find the relative speed of two spacecraft in their common plane, using 365 days per year.

children.text: Force balance for either mass, together with the centre-of-mass relation, gives \[\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{(R+r)^3}}.\]

In the co-rotating configuration, the acceleration is \(-\omega_0^2\mathbf r_\mu\). Equate this to the vector sum of the two gravitational accelerations. Comparing coefficients of the two nonparallel relative-position vectors using \(M\mathbf r_M+m\mathbf r_m=0\) gives equal inverse-cube distances to the two masses, each equal to \((R+r)^{-3}\). Thus the triangle is equilateral and both distances are R + r.
The same equilateral configuration gives R + r. There are two mirror positions, the usual triangular Lagrange points.
Use the cosine rule in a triangle with sides r and R+r and included angle \(60^\circ\): \[\rho=\sqrt{R^2+Rr+r^2}.\]

Here R = r and \(\rho_0=\sqrt3R\). In the stipulated radial model the attraction is \(-2GM\rho/(R^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}\). Conserved angular momentum gives centrifugal term \(\rho_0^4\omega_0^2/\rho^3\). Linearizing their sum around \(\rho_0\) yields \[\ddot\xi=-\frac74\omega_0^2\xi,\qquad\omega_{rad}=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}\omega_0.\] This is the restricted radial calculation requested. It does not establish stability of the unrestricted equal-mass triangular three-body configuration.

For rigid rotation in the triangle plane, the relative-position vector has fixed length L and rotates with \(\omega=2\pi/T\). Hence \[v_{rel}=\omega L=\frac{2\pi(5.0\times10^9\,\mathrm m)}{365\times86400\,\mathrm s}=996\,\mathrm{m/s}.\] The common heliocentric translation cancels. These are the mission parameters supplied in the historical problem, not a statement of the current mission design.

solution.text:
A Three-body Problem and LISA
1.1. Binary angular velocity
Force balance for either mass, together with the centre-of-mass relation, gives \[\omega_0=\sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{(R+r)^3}}.\]
1.2.1. Distance to M
In the co-rotating configuration, the acceleration is \(-\omega_0^2\mathbf r_\mu\). Equate this to the vector sum of the two gravitational accelerations. Comparing coefficients of the two nonparallel relative-position vectors using \(M\mathbf r_M+m\mathbf r_m=0\) gives equal inverse-cube distances to the two masses, each equal to \((R+r)^{-3}\). Thus the triangle is equilateral and both distances are R + r.
1.2.2. Distance to m
The same equilateral configuration gives R + r. There are two mirror positions, the usual triangular Lagrange points.
1.2.3. Distance to O
Use the cosine rule in a triangle with sides r and R+r and included angle \(60^\circ\): \[\rho=\sqrt{R^2+Rr+r^2}.\]
1.3. Restricted radial oscillation
Here R = r and \(\rho_0=\sqrt3R\). In the stipulated radial model the attraction is \(-2GM\rho/(R^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}\). Conserved angular momentum gives centrifugal term \(\rho_0^4\omega_0^2/\rho^3\). Linearizing their sum around \(\rho_0\) yields \[\ddot\xi=-\frac74\omega_0^2\xi,\qquad\omega_{rad}=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}\omega_0.\] This is the restricted radial calculation requested. It does not establish stability of the unrestricted equal-mass triangular three-body configuration.
1.4. LISA relative speed
For rigid rotation in the triangle plane, the relative-position vector has fixed length L and rotates with \(\omega=2\pi/T\). Hence \[v_{rel}=\omega L=\frac{2\pi(5.0\times10^9\,\mathrm m)}{365\times86400\,\mathrm s}=996\,\mathrm{m/s}.\] The common heliocentric translation cancels. These are the mission parameters supplied in the historical problem, not a statement of the current mission design.
